findings.issue_text: [BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor()/math.ceil() directly on getattr(item, self.key), which is a datetime object for this endpoint (key is derived from order_by='-datetime'), whereas DateTimePaginator.get_item_key converts via value.timestamp() first. Every request to the audit-logs endpoint with optimized_pagination=true that returns at least one row raises TypeError ('type datetime.datetime doesn't define __floor__ method') inside build_cursor (which calls key(results[0])), so the entire optimized path 500s on its first use — the feature is dead on arrival.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value instead of converting the timestamp back to a datetime (DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor does datetime.fromtimestamp(float(cursor.value))), so build_queryset (line 857) filters datetime__gt=<int>. Any optimized request carrying a cursor (page 2+ navigation, or a hand-crafted cursor like cursor=1712345678:0:0) fails when Django's DateTimeField prepares the integer for comparison — to_python raises during query compilation at list(queryset[...]) — returning a 500 instead of the next page.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start (queryset[start_offset:stop] with start_offset<0), which Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly forbids — it raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.') — contradicting the comment's claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'; the adjacent 'safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' comment is also false, since authorization lives in the endpoint's permission_classes, not the queryset. An admin sending a negative-offset cursor (e.g. cursor=0:-5:0) with optimized_pagination=true gets a 500 from an uncaught AssertionError; the same cursor on the non-optimized path is clamped to page 1 by the modified BasePaginator.get_result, so the 'optimized' path is strictly worse than the path it replaces.

[ADVISORY] The clamp added to the shared BasePaginator.get_result changes malformed-cursor handling for every paginated endpoint in Sentry, not just audit logs: forward cursors with negative offsets now silently return page 1 (previously AssertionError/500) while prev cursors with negative offsets still raise AssertionError, and the added comment's claim that 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' is false for the is_prev branch. API clients sending malformed cursors get silent page-1 data instead of an error on every list endpoint fleet-wide, masking client bugs; the forward/prev inconsistency and the false safety comment will mislead the next maintainer of this heavily shared code path.

[ADVISORY] The new paginator delivers none of the promised performance work: it inherits build_queryset unchanged and executes the identical query and slicing as the existing DateTimePaginator path, so the docstring's 'Optimized query path for large datasets' describes a capability that does not exist anywhere in the diff. Reviewers and operators merge a 'performance' PR that adds a broken parallel code path and permanent maintenance burden with zero performance benefit; any real optimization (index, query shape, caching) still remains to be written.

[ADVISORY] get_result is a ~65-line copy of BasePaginator.get_result with only one branch changed, and the copy has already drifted from its source (cursor_value defaults to 0 where BasePaginator uses None). Future fixes to BasePaginator.get_result (hits accounting, boundary handling, cursor construction) will not propagate to this copy, producing divergent pagination behavior between the optimized and standard paths; extracting the negative-offset handling as a hook would make the entire duplicate block unnecessary.

[ADVISORY] No test in this diff exercises any of the new logic — the OptimizedCursorPaginator class, its negative-offset branch, and the endpoint's optimized_pagination/enable_advanced gating are all untested. Each of the three crashes above (TypeError in get_item_key, integer-vs-datetime filter failure, negative-slice AssertionError) would have been caught by a single request-level test against the audit-logs endpoint; without tests, any fix to this class can regress silently.

[ADVISORY] The admin gate uses request.user.is_superuser (the static model flag) instead of request.is_superuser, the session-scoped signal that Sentry's SuperuserMiddleware and the Access object used by this endpoint's own permission_classes rely on for superuser powers. A superuser who has not activated superuser mode passes this gate and receives the 'advanced' pagination path, inconsistent with how the rest of the API scopes superuser privileges; the gate's correctness also silently depends on short-circuit evaluation hiding the fact that organization_context.member is Optional.

[BUG] The new permission gate references `organization_context`, a name that is neither imported nor assigned anywhere in this diff, and the expression `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally on every GET to the endpoint. Every request to the audit-log endpoint (including requests that never send optimized_pagination) raises NameError and returns a 500 instead of the 200 the endpoint contract promises — the whole endpoint goes down, not just the new feature.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil directly to `getattr(item, self.key)`, which resolves to the AuditLogEntry `datetime` attribute (a datetime object) because the endpoint passes order_by='-datetime' and BasePaginator derives key='datetime' from it. math.ceil(datetime) raises TypeError ('type datetime.datetime doesn't define __ceil__ method') inside build_cursor, which calls get_item_key on the results, so every optimized_pagination request that returns any rows fails with a 500 — the new paginator cannot serve a single non-empty page.

[BUG] The 'advanced' negative-offset branch slices the Django QuerySet with a negative start index (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` with start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), but Django's QuerySet raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.') for negative slice bounds — the inline premise that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any administrator exercising the advertised feature (a cursor with negative offset, e.g. '0:-5:0') gets a 500 AssertionError; the flagship capability this PR exists to deliver crashes on first use.

[BUG] The diff contains no mechanism that improves pagination performance: OptimizedCursorPaginator reuses BasePaginator's generic build_queryset and slicing (and replaces DateTimePaginator's datetime-aware value_from_cursor conversion with raw-epoch passthrough), so the PR's stated requirement — faster pagination for high-volume audit logs — has no implementing change anywhere in the diff. Operators who enable optimized_pagination get the same database cost as the existing path (plus the new 500s from the crashing branches); the acceptance criterion promised by the PR title is silently unmet and nothing in the diff measures or verifies any performance gain.

[BUG] No test files exist anywhere in this diff (only the three source files are touched — no spec/**, test/**, or *.spec.* paths), yet the diff adds ~95 lines of new paginator behavior, a new endpoint branch, and modifies the shared BasePaginator.get_result slicing used by every cursor-paginated endpoint. Nothing verifies the optimized_pagination branch, negative-offset cursors, or prev-cursor behavior after the slicing change; a regression in the shared slicing change would silently break pagination across all cursor-paginated endpoints with no failing test to catch it.

[ADVISORY] `optimized_pagination` is gated only by a raw query-string comparison (`request.GET.get(...) == "true"`) with no feature flag or options entry; the role check is authorization, not rollout control. When the optimized path misbehaves in production (it does — it 500s per the findings above), operators cannot disable it without a code deploy; exposure is controlled only by whoever happens to be a superuser or global-access member.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a ~60-line verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result with one branch added, and this same diff already had to duplicate the new max(0, offset) clamp into the copy to keep the two in sync. Every future fix to BasePaginator.get_result must be manually mirrored here or the two paginators drift; the deletion test passes cleanly — removing the class and the endpoint branch removes the duplicate entirely, since the base path already serves this endpoint.

[ADVISORY] The clamp `max(0, offset)` silently changes shared paginator behavior for every cursor-paginated endpoint: a client-supplied negative offset on a non-prev cursor previously raised AssertionError (500) via negative slicing and now silently returns results from offset 0. API consumers sending malformed cursors now receive page-1 data instead of an error, masking client pagination bugs; the API contract change is unflagged, untested, and unrelated to the PR's stated audit-log scope.

[BUG] Line 71 references `organization_context`, which is not imported in this module's import block and is not defined as a local anywhere in the diff, so the assignment `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises NameError. Because this line executes unconditionally (outside the `use_optimized` branch), every GET to the audit-log listing endpoint returns 500 for all callers — admins and regular members alike — the moment this code deploys, taking down the pre-existing default path along with the new one.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result performs the identical cursor-window queryset slicing (`queryset[start_offset:stop]`) as the existing Paginator.get_result — there is no query-level optimization anywhere in the diff (no keyset/index change, no reduced counting, no cheaper query shape). The PR's stated intent — pagination performance for high-volume audit logs — is not implemented: the default DateTimePaginator path is unchanged, and the opt-in path issues the same LIMIT/OFFSET-shaped query, so high-volume consumers receive zero performance improvement plus a new broken code path to maintain.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator extends BasePaginator but never assigns `self.queryset`, `self.key`, `self.desc`, `self.on_results`, or `self.post_query_filter` and never defines `build_queryset`/`count_hits` — the constructor forwards `queryset`/`order_by`/`on_results` into BasePaginator's ignored **kwargs — so the first optimized-path request raises AttributeError (at `self.max_limit`, `self.build_queryset`, or `self.key`). Every authorized admin request with `?optimized_pagination=true` fails with a 500 AttributeError; the feature shipped as the PR's centerpiece is dead code that cannot execute a single request.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` with `start_offset < 0`), which Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ rejects with `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` — the inline claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any authorized admin who presents a cursor with a negative offset on the optimized path gets a 500 instead of the promised 'efficient traversal of large datasets'; the branch cannot ever succeed, so the advanced feature is broken by construction.

[ADVISORY] This hunk modifies the shared Paginator.get_result used by every paginated endpoint in Sentry, clamping negative forward-cursor offsets to 0, even though the new audit-log feature uses a separate class that does not inherit this method — the change is traceable to no requirement in this PR. Platform-wide silent behavior change: crafted negative-offset forward cursors on any endpoint now silently return page-0 results instead of erroring, while negative-offset prev cursors still raise AssertionError — an inconsistent half-change shipped to all of Sentry to support a single-endpoint opt-in feature.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds an undocumented, client-controlled `optimized_pagination` query parameter that switches pagination implementation based on caller privilege (`is_superuser`/`has_global_access`), with no feature-flag or option backing. API consumers cannot discover or document the parameter; non-admin callers who pass it get silent fallback with no signal; operators cannot roll it out or disable it per-organization without a code deploy; and tying a pagination mode to admin privilege is traceable to no stated requirement — a performance fix should not be a hidden superuser-only mode.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a ~60-line verbatim copy of Paginator.get_result with one added branch, and the copy has already drifted: get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil directly to the attribute value, dropping the `.timestamp()` conversion the datetime-based paginators perform. Future fixes to Paginator.get_result (boundary handling, hits accounting) will not reach the copy, and if the class were ever wired with a datetime key, `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError; the negative-offset need could have been met by subclassing the existing Paginator instead of duplicating it.

[ADVISORY] The diff ships new non-trivial logic — the shared Paginator offset clamp, the full OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, the negative-offset branch, and the endpoint's privilege-gated branch — with no test changes anywhere in the diff. A regression in the shared clamp at line 182 would silently change pagination behavior on every list endpoint in Sentry with nothing to catch it; the admin gate and the negative-offset branch are likewise unverifiable, so the broken paths above would pass CI unnoticed.

[ADVISORY] The `enable_advanced` privilege evaluation executes unconditionally on every request, including the default DateTimePaginator path that this diff otherwise leaves unchanged. The high-volume default path the PR claims to optimize gains a new per-request privilege evaluation and a hard dependency on `organization_context`; any failure in that expression takes down the default path too, not just the opt-in path.

[ADVISORY] This hunk adds only comments claiming Cursor now 'allows negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios', but no behavior changes — `int(offset)` already accepted negative values before this diff. Future readers of the shared cursor utility are told a capability change happened here that did not, sending them hunting for behavior that actually lives (broken) in paginator.py; the comment is untraceable work product in a shared module.

[ADVISORY] The new behavior is routed through three parallel booleans (`use_optimized` query param, `enable_advanced` privilege check, `enable_advanced_features` constructor flag), and the constructor flag is speculative generality — its single call site always passes True. Maintainers must reason about a three-flag matrix to trace one behavior, and the flag's only effect is selecting the negative-offset branch that raises AssertionError; deleting the flag and branch removes a dead decision point with no loss of function.

[ADVISORY] The two branches contain duplicate `self.paginate(...)` call blocks differing only in `paginator_cls` and the extra kwarg, where a single call with a conditionally selected paginator class would suffice. Any future change to the shared pagination parameters (e.g., adding count_hits or changing on_results) must be applied in two places in this method or the optimized and default paths silently diverge.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator carries Paginator's numeric-key cursor semantics — get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil to getattr(item, self.key) and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value — with none of the datetime↔numeric conversions DateTimePaginator provides, yet its only call site orders audit logs by -datetime, so build_cursor's key(results[-1]) calls math.ceil on a datetime and raises TypeError. Every request with optimized_pagination=true from an authorized admin against an org with at least one matching audit event returns a 500 instead of the audit page; even if the key resolved differently, the class defines no datetime-aware value_from_cursor, so page≥2 would filter the datetime column against a raw int — the optimized path cannot produce a successful paginated response in any configuration, making the shipped feature dead on arrival.

[BUG] The enable_advanced_features branch slices the queryset with a negative start (queryset[start_offset:stop] where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), which Django's ORM explicitly rejects with 'Negative indexing is not supported', directly contradicting the adjacent comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. Any admin sending a cursor with a negative offset (e.g. cursor=0:-3:0, which Cursor.from_string parses happily) under optimized_pagination=true gets a 500; since the negative-offset branch is the only code the enable_advanced_features flag activates, the 'advanced features' toggle's sole behavioral effect is enabling a crash path.

[BUG] The clamp added to the shared Paginator.get_result changes slicing semantics for every cursor-paginated endpoint in the codebase — non-prev cursors with negative offsets previously raised (Django rejects negative slices) and now silently return first-page data, while prev cursors with negative offsets still raise — and the change is not load-bearing for the audit-log feature since the new paginator class carries its own copy of this logic. All endpoints backed by Paginator/DateTimePaginator inherit new behavior for malformed cursors (silent clamp to page 1 instead of an error) with no test or rollout gate, and the same malformed cursor now diverges by direction: next navigation silently returns page-1 rows mislabeled as the requested position while prev navigation 500s.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates ~60 lines of Paginator.get_result verbatim (offset/extra computation, prev-cursor trim, build_cursor wiring, post_query_filter) and is behaviorally identical to the base path outside the crash branch, so pagination semantics are now maintained in two hand-synced copies that already diverge in this very diff (the base clamps negative non-prev offsets; the copy's advanced branch does not). Every future fix to cursor pagination (off-by-one in the prev trim, hits handling, key normalization) must be applied in two places or the two paginators silently drift; the correct shape is subclassing Paginator and overriding only the delta — or no new class at all, since the only delta is a crash.

[ADVISORY] The docstring claims an 'Optimized query path for large datasets', but no code in the diff changes data access: the optimized path executes the same queryset, the same OFFSET-based slice (queryset[start_offset:stop]), and the same serialization as the legacy DateTimePaginator path, so the diff's stated purpose — performance for high-volume audit logs — is implemented nowhere. Maintainers carry forward a new class, a public query param, and a privilege fork under the belief that audit-log pagination performance improved, while the actual high-volume cost (deep-page OFFSET scans over the audit table, which the slice arithmetic still performs) remains unaddressed; the real fix — pure keyset pagination without OFFSET — is absent.

[ADVISORY] Pagination behavior for the same endpoint and the same cursor strings now forks on caller identity (request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access) toggled by an undocumented raw query param, reusing a data-scope privilege (has_global_access) as a gate for a pagination feature it has no semantic relationship to. A cursor string shared between an admin and a member (links, exports, integrations) resolves through different code paths with different failure semantics — member: silently clamped legacy path; admin: the 500-prone optimized path — and there is no options/feature-flag entry to disable or stage the behavior, only a code deploy; the strongest author counter ('it is opt-in and admin-only') fails because opt-in via a raw param is itself the new public contract and identity-dependent pagination breaks cursor stability.

[ADVISORY] The added comment claims the unchanged self.offset assignment 'enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets', but no code in this diff implements negative-offset traversal and Django rejects negative queryset slices, so the comment documents a nonexistent capability on the exact field the crash branch in paginator.py depends on. The next maintainer reading Cursor.offset's only documentation will treat negative offsets as a supported, efficient mode and build on it, reproducing the 500 branch; the comment is newly written misinformation, not stale doc.

[ADVISORY] The diff's new branching pagination logic — the global clamp in Paginator.get_result, the advanced negative-offset branch, and the entire OptimizedCursorPaginator class — ships with no test in the diff, leaving both the clamp's cross-endpoint behavior change and the optimized path's datetime TypeError unexercised. A regression in the shared clamp would silently alter cursor pagination for every paginated endpoint without CI noticing, and the dead-on-arrival optimized path would first surface as an admin-hit 500 in production; a single request-level test with a datetime-ordered queryset would have caught it.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil directly to getattr(item, self.key), which for the endpoint's order_by='-datetime' is a datetime object, so the first optimized request that returns any results raises TypeError inside build_cursor (key=self.get_item_key at line 904). Every GET to the audit-log endpoint with optimized_pagination=true from an authorized admin returns a 500 instead of a page — the new pagination mode fails on its very first use, so the shipped feature is dead on arrival.

[BUG] The advanced negative-offset branch executes queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start_offset, which Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ rejects with AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported') — the branch's own comment ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') is factually false. Any optimized-pagination request carrying a negative-offset cursor — the exact reverse-pagination case this branch and the class docstring were built for — crashes with a 500; the feature's core mechanism cannot work as designed.

[BUG] The diff rewrites the shared Paginator.get_result slicing used by every Paginator/DateTimePaginator endpoint in Sentry: a client-supplied non-prev cursor with negative offset (e.g. cursor=0:-5:0, parseable from the cursor query param) previously reached queryset[-5:stop] and raised (500), and now silently clamps to offset 0 and returns the first page — a global behavior change the audit-logs objective never required (the new paginator overrides get_result entirely) and one that contradicts its own comment, which claims to 'allow' negative offsets while actually clamping them. Every paginated endpoint silently changes how crafted cursors behave (500 → silent first page), and a negative-offset cursor emitted by the optimized mode and replayed without the flag (or against a pre-deploy worker) resolves to the wrong page silently instead of failing loudly; this global semantic change was never part of the accepted objective.

[BUG] The new enable_advanced line dereferences organization_context.member.has_global_access, but organization_context is defined nowhere in the diff or in the visible body of get() (the pre-diff code never references it), and the line executes unconditionally on every GET rather than only inside the optimized branch. Every non-superuser request to the audit-log endpoint raises NameError and returns 500 — the previously working default path is broken, not just the new branch.

[BUG] The artifact no longer matches its stated objective: nothing in the diff improves pagination performance (the optimized path performs the identical offset-sliced query against the same queryset), and the delivered change is a new admin-only pagination mode toggled by an undocumented raw query parameter (optimized_pagination) with no feature flag — an objective substitution that was never explicitly accepted. Reviewers and operators accepting 'pagination performance for high-volume audit logs' silently ship a privileged alternate execution path on a public endpoint that cannot be disabled without a code deploy, while the stated performance goal remains entirely unmet.

[ADVISORY] The modified shared slicing in Paginator.get_result, the new negative-offset branch, and the admin gate all ship with no test anywhere in the diff. A regression in this shared slicing code silently breaks pagination offset math on every endpoint using Paginator/DateTimePaginator (projects, issues, members, etc.) with nothing in CI to catch it; the highest-blast-radius change in the PR is also its least-verified.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator copy-pastes ~40 lines of Paginator.get_result while inheriting from BasePaginator, whose contract does not provide the build_queryset/count_hits/on_results members the copy calls, and Sentry already ships CursorPaginator (the class whose get_result tail this hunk appends after) for exactly this keyset-style pagination use case. Every future fix to the base paginator's cursor arithmetic must be manually replicated in this copy, which the diff itself already shows drifting from its source (different negative-offset handling); deleting the class in favor of the existing CursorPaginator removes the entire duplicated and partially non-functional surface.

[ADVISORY] The same endpoint now serves two paginators with different cursor value derivations selected by a client-controlled query parameter, so cursor tokens issued under optimized_pagination=true are not portable to the default path (different get_item_key/value_from_cursor semantics) or to workers running the prior code during a rolling deploy. Audit-log consumers that paginate programmatically and drop or lose the optimized_pagination parameter (or hit a pre-deploy worker) feed cursors across incompatible paginators and get wrong pages or errors depending on direction — for an audit trail, silently skipped or duplicated pages are a compliance problem.

[BUG] Line 71 dereferences `organization_context`, a name that appears nowhere else in this file and is absent from the module's import block shown in this diff, so for non-superusers (who do not short-circuit past it via `request.user.is_superuser`) the expression evaluates an undefined name. Every GET to the organization audit-log endpoint by a non-superuser raises NameError and returns HTTP 500; because the expression is evaluated unconditionally before the `use_optimized` branch, the endpoint is down for its entire regular membership even for callers who never request optimized pagination.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` on a Django QuerySet, and Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` for any negative slice bound — the in-code claim that the ORM 'handles negative slicing automatically' is false. An admin sending a cursor with a negative offset (e.g. `?optimized_pagination=true&cursor=0:-1:0`) triggers an unhandled AssertionError and gets a 500 on every such request; the `max(0, offset)` clamp that prevents exactly this input is explicitly bypassed on this path, making the new 'advanced' mode a client-input-driven crash path rather than a pagination feature.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` to the raw attribute value, but this endpoint paginates with `order_by='-datetime'`, so `self.key` resolves to `datetime` and the value is a datetime object, which `math.floor` rejects with TypeError. The very first optimized-pagination request (no cursor required) crashes inside build_cursor when it keys the last result to build the next cursor, returning a 500; the feature is dead on arrival and every admin attempt to use it produces a server error.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten clamp `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` still feeds a negative offset straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]` for prev cursors, so the comment added on this change ('This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions') is false for the prev branch. A crafted prev cursor carrying a negative offset (e.g. `cursor=0:-1:1`) still raises Django's AssertionError and returns 500 on any endpoint using BasePaginator.get_result; the diff rewrote this exact line, asserted its safety, and left the unvalidated-offset crash in place one branch over instead of clamping both paths.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator inherits BasePaginator.build_queryset and defines value_from_cursor to return the raw integer cursor value, omitting the epoch-to-datetime conversion DateTimePaginator performs before filtering, so any page after the first compares the `datetime` column against a raw integer. Once the first-page crash is fixed, every subsequent page issues a timestamp-vs-integer comparison that the database rejects (or silently mis-filters), meaning the paginator cannot actually traverse the datetime-ordered audit-log queryset it was built for.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a ~65-line verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result differing only in the negative-offset branch, creating a second hand-maintained copy of the pagination core instead of overriding a single hook. Future fixes or hardening applied to BasePaginator.get_result — including the offset clamp added in this same diff — silently will not apply to the optimized path that serves audit-log access, leaving a diverging, less-reviewed copy of pagination logic guarding who-sees-what ordering in production.

[BUG] The new gate `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` references `organization_context`, a name that is neither imported in this module (the diff adds only the paginator import) nor defined in `get()`'s scope — it matches the sentry.testutils test-fixture shape (`organization_context.member`), not any production API available to this endpoint. The line sits outside the `use_optimized` branch so it executes on every GET, and the `or` short-circuit only spares superusers; every authenticated non-superuser request to the audit-log listing endpoint raises NameError and returns a 500 — a full outage of the endpoint for regular users, which any test of a normal (non-superuser) request would have caught immediately.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key raises on every invocation: it calls `self._is_asc(for_prev)`, a method defined nowhere in OptimizedCursorPaginator and not part of the BasePaginator interface the existing paginators in this module use, and it applies `math.floor(value)`/`math.ceil(value)` directly to the `datetime` key value (from `order_by="-datetime"`), dropping the `.timestamp()` conversion that DateTimePaginator.get_item_key performs on the same key. build_cursor calls get_item_key on the first and last row of every non-empty page (and the prev-trim block calls it for prev cursors), so the first admin request with `?optimized_pagination=true` that returns any row fails with AttributeError or TypeError inside get_result and the endpoint returns a 500 — the optimized path fails on 100% of real invocations, something a single smoke test of the new branch would have exposed.

[BUG] The 'advanced' negative-offset branch slices the Django QuerySet with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = cursor.offset < 0`), which Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly forbids by raising `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` — the inline premise 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false, so the branch crashes every time it executes. Any superuser or global-access member who sends `?optimized_pagination=true` with a cursor carrying a negative offset (e.g. `?cursor=0:-5:0`, accepted by Cursor's plain `int(offset)` parse per the cursors.py hunk) gets a 500; the advertised negative-offset support — the entire stated reason this paginator exists — never completes a single request.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a ~65-line copy of Paginator.get_result instead of a subclass override, and the copy has already drifted from its source in three places: get_item_key drops the `.timestamp()` conversion, value_from_cursor returns the raw numeric cursor value that build_queryset then compares against the `datetime` DateTimeField (a timestamp-vs-datetime mismatch on any cursor-filtered page), and `is_asc` is invoked as `_is_asc`. The drift is not hypothetical — it is exactly what breaks the class — and every future change to Paginator.get_result (hits handling, boundary trimming, cursor building) must now be replicated by hand in this second copy or the two paginators silently diverge; subclassing Paginator/DateTimePaginator and overriding only the offset-slicing step would delete the duplicated block and its drift surface.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator is speculative generality: its query path is identical to the existing Paginator's (same build_queryset, same offset/limit windowing, same build_cursor), so the 'performance optimization for high-traffic endpoints' has no mechanism that could make any query faster — the only behavioral delta it adds is the crashing negative-offset branch. ~95 lines of admin-gated, opt-in code (this class plus the endpoint branch plus the base-paginator tweak) are added to serve a pattern no client uses and that cannot deliver the claimed benefit; deleting the class, the `optimized_pagination` branch, and the base-paginator change removes both crash sites and the NameError gate while losing nothing, which is the correct resolution rather than repairing the copy.
